headline: mixed
texts: You hold part of this topic firmly and part is still loose. The pattern in breast cancer is that many exam keys changed (core biopsy, N3c, MRM or BCS), so a loose area usually means an old key is still active. Start with the objectives marked below, then the review cards.

Most-common answers are partly secure. Fix the three anchors: breast cancer now leads in India, upper outer quadrant is the commonest site, invasive ductal NST is the commonest type. Redo the O1 card.

Lobular versus ductal or the BRCA pairs are partly secure. Keep the two sets apart: lobular means single file, bilateral, odd metastatic sites; BRCA2 means 13q and male breast cancer. Redo the O2 card.
Work-up choices are partly secure. Say the reason aloud: core biopsy gives histology and receptors, FNAC is kept for nodes and cysts, and age picks ultrasound or mammography. Redo the O3 card.
Staging scans are partly secure. Tie the scan to stage and symptoms, not to where metastases usually go. Bone is common, node status is the main prognostic factor. Redo the O4 card.
T category is partly secure. Keep the T4 set apart: ribs, intercostals and serratus are T4a, skin signs are T4b, T4d needs the inflammatory picture. Redo the O5 card.
N and M are partly secure. Rehearse the ladder by position: axilla N1 or N2a, internal mammary N2b, infraclavicular N3a, supraclavicular N3c. Redo the O6 card.

Operation choice is partly secure. Hold the contrast: MRM spares pectoralis major, Halsted removes it and pectoralis minor, and BCS plus radiotherapy matches mastectomy for survival in suitable cases. Redo the O7 card.

Surgical decisions are partly secure. Build the BCS contraindications from logic (multicentric, prior radiotherapy, pregnancy, persistent positive margins) and keep SLNB for cN0 and ALND for node-positive. Redo the O8 card.
Treatment sequence is partly secure. Rehearse the order with its reason: chemotherapy first to downstage and treat spread, then MRM, then radiotherapy. Redo the O9 card.
Hormonal therapy is partly secure. Re-read the qualifier each time: premenopausal means tamoxifen, postmenopausal means aromatase inhibitor, and tamoxifen carries endometrial risk. Redo the O10 card.
The HER2 drug is partly secure. Keep the pair apart: trastuzumab is reversible and not dose-related, doxorubicin is cumulative and largely irreversible. Redo the O11 card.

Axillary dissection complications are partly secure. Pair each nerve to its deficit, then separate frequency from drama: intercostobrachial is commonest, long thoracic is the dramatic one. Redo the O12 card.
You moved from the old FNAC key to core biopsy. It can return under pressure, so ask each time what the pathologist must report.
You replaced the old M1 key with N3c. Under pressure the old key can return, so place the node on the ladder by position first.
You updated from Halsted to BCS plus radiotherapy or MRM. The urge to pick the biggest operation can return, so ask what survival data support.
You dropped the cervix key for breast. The remembered PYQ can come back under pressure, so check whether epidemiology has changed.
You moved from scanning everyone to scanning by stage and symptoms. The bone-metastasis link can pull you back, so check stage first.
You separated trastuzumab from doxorubicin. Both are cardiotoxic, so the merge can return, so recall dose relation and reversibility each time.
You began reading menopausal status instead of stopping at ER-positive. Exam stems may hide the status, so look for it first.
You moved off the ductal default to lobular where the stem showed single-file cells. The pull of 'commonest' can return, so read the pattern.
You stopped tying peau d'orange to T4d. The reverse error can appear in an inflammatory stem, so ask for the clinical picture.
You removed pectoralis from the T4a list. Muscle fixity is a tempting cue, so rebuild the list from ribs, intercostals and serratus.
You dropped size alone from the contraindications. Size relative to the breast, and downstaging, can mislead again, so ask whether margins and radiotherapy are possible.
You separated the commonest nerve injury from the most dramatic one. Winging is vivid and can return, so pair each nerve to its deficit.
You moved the operation behind neoadjuvant chemotherapy in advanced disease. Surgery feels decisive and can return under pressure, so ask what must come first.
You separated 'most common cause' from 'cause to exclude'. The alarm of bloody discharge can pull you back to carcinoma, so keep the qualifier.
You fixed the order to SLNB in clinically node-negative disease. The old dissect-first habit can return, so ask what the axilla needs.
You re-anchored the BRCA numbers. Number pairs fade quickly, so rehearse them again before the exam.
You fixed the gene and phenotype pairs. BRCA1 is the famous one and can return as the default, so read which phenotype the stem describes.
You began checking age before choosing imaging. The screening test can slip back in, so ask age and breast density first.
You corrected the reversed mechanism. Tamoxifen blocks the breast but acts partly as an agonist in the uterus, so predict each tissue separately.
You changed from operating on classic LCIS to surveillance. 'Carcinoma in situ' can still tempt you, so ask what the lesion predicts.
You tend to answer with an older PYQ key (cervix, FNAC, Halsted, M1). Ask whether practice or staging has changed, and keep both answers ready: what PYQs expected and what current practice says.
You tend to stop reading at the diagnosis and miss the qualifier, such as menopausal status, age or setting. Underline the qualifier in the stem before choosing a drug or test.
You tend to merge look-alikes and match on one sign, such as peau d'orange or the commonest histology. Before answering, name the one feature that separates the pair, then check the stem has it.
You tend to add familiar items to fixed lists, such as pectoralis in T4a or size in BCS contraindications. Rebuild each list from its logic, not from what looks related.
You tend to link a gene or nerve to its most famous association rather than the one the stem describes. Pair each with its phenotype or deficit and separate common from dramatic.
You tend to name the right steps in the wrong order, with surgery or dissection first. Ask what comes first and why before sequencing.

You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. High-confidence errors are the best-remembered once fixed, so review those cards first and pause for one beat before tapping Sure on staging or surgery questions.
You asked for hints or explanations often. That is a sound way to learn new material, but the exam gives none. Redo the review cards without opening a hint, starting with the objectives marked shaky.
Start with the cards for objectives marked gap, beginning with any trap you fell into while sure. Do one card per day on a 1, 3, 7 day schedule, then replay the segment for the weakest objective.
